Efficient Test-Time Inference via Deterministic Exploration of Truncated Decoding Trees

Xueyan Li    Johannes Zenn    Ekaterina Fadeeva    Guinan Su    Mrinmaya Sachan   Jonas Geiping Affiliation: Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems Affiliation: ETH Zurich Affiliation: AI Center Tübingen Affiliation: University of Tübingen Affiliation: ELLIS Institute Tübingen Affiliation: IMPRS-IS
Abstract

Self-consistency boosts inference-time performance by sampling multiple reasoning traces in parallel and voting. However, in constrained domains like math and code, this strategy is compute-inefficient because it samples with replacement, repeatedly revisiting the same high-probability prefixes and duplicate completions. We propose Distinct Leaf Enumeration (DLE), a deterministic decoding method that treats truncated sampling as traversal of a pruned decoding tree and systematically enumerates distinct leaves instead of sampling with replacement. This strategy improves inference efficiency in two ways. Algorithmically, it increases coverage of the truncated search space under a fixed budget by exploring previously unvisited high-probability branches. Systemically, it reuses shared prefixes and reduces redundant token generation. Empirically, DLE explores higher-quality reasoning traces than stochastic self-consistency, yielding better performance on math, coding, and general reasoning tasks.

1 Introduction

Parallel test-time computation has emerged as a principled way of scaling the performance of large language models (LLMs) (Snell et al., 2024; Lin et al., 2024). By sampling multiple solution traces for the same prompt and aggregating them via majority voting or answer-weighted selection (Wang et al., 2024a; Taubenfeld et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2023), additional inference time compute can be used for performance gains. However, naive stochastic sampling of multiple solutions is inefficient. For constrained domains like math and coding where problems are only solved by a narrow set of viable solutions, similar reasoning steps are repeatedly generated (Zhu et al., 2024; Gao et al., 2025; Hong et al., 2025).

Figure 1 (top) shows this redundancy where three out of five generations are the same (first three rows), and four out of five generations share a prefix. Figure 2 makes this more concrete by showing the repetition rate among prefixes: we find that for code generation, 20%20\% of all prefix tokens are repeated across generated traces. Thinking of generated sequences in terms of a tree structure, this means that early branches are repeatedly traversed. At the same time, the number of possible continuations grows exponentially per generated token. This makes search efficiency critical.

Classical search methods such as beam search (Lowerre, 1976; Sutskever et al., 2014) make this tree structure explicit and control the traversed range with their number of branches (beams). However, beam search results in degenerate repetitions (Vijayakumar et al., 2016; Cohen and Beck, 2019), quality deterioration with larger beams (Koehn and Knowles, 2017; Yang et al., 2018) and a lack of diversity (Su et al., 2022).

In this work, we argue that effective tree-based generation for modern LLMs requires two practical ingredients, a principled way to truncate the exponentially large tree of possible completions, and a good heuristic for partial exploration under a limited compute budget. Since the full decoding tree is intractable, the tree size can be reduced by a truncated next-token distribution. Common truncated samplers such as top-kk (Fan et al., 2018), top-pp (nucleus sampling) (Holtzman et al., 2020), min-pp (Minh et al., 2025) and ε\varepsilon-sampling (Hewitt et al., 2022), are widely used to stabilize generation with a restricted set of candidate tokens at each decoding step (Li et al., 2026). Unlike beam search, which considers alternatives at every position, truncation-based sampling branches only when multiple valid tokens survive the truncation rule. Modern post-trained models are overconfident (Tian et al., 2023; Leng et al., 2025), often exhibiting sharpened output distributions. Thus, only a few tokens survive truncation at each step which reduces the effective tree size.

Motivated by these observations, we propose Distinct Leaf Enumeration (DLE), an alternative to (sampled) self-consistency that minimizes repetitions via tree search. DLE enumerates distinct leaves in the truncated generation tree by choosing deterministically which tokens to explore instead of sampling from the vocabulary probability distribution. The output is a set of distinct reasoning chains that never generate duplicate traces. This makes DLE a natural replacement for self-consistency in settings where repeated sampling is especially wasteful, such as in code synthesis and tightly specified math problems.

DLE differs from prior decoding and search methods in both objective and mechanism. Unlike beam-style methods (Sutskever et al., 2014; Vijayakumar et al., 2016), it does not maintain diverse partial beams at each step. Unlike sampling-without-replacement methods (Kool et al., 2019; Shi et al., 2021), it is not designed to preserve a target sampling distribution. Unlike tree-of-thought (Yao et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2025) style branching, it requires no additional deliberation or evaluation calls. Instead, DLE deterministically enumerates distinct leaves of a truncated decoding tree to improve coverage under a fixed compute budget.

Further, DLE is able to reuse generated prefixes. Since it expands a pruned tree, it never re-generates the same prefix and lowers the number of newly generated tokens for the same number of sequences compared to self-consistency.

In this paper, we propose DLE, as a deterministic enumeration method independent of the truncated sampling distribution. Empirically, at equal token budgets, DLE covers more probability space than self-consistency, translating to better performance. This also results in reduced inference time especially in memory-constrained conditions. Our main contributions are:

  • •

    We propose Distinct Leaf Enumeration (DLE), a repetition-free decoding method as a deterministic drop-in replacement for stochastic sampling. It applies broadly to samplers such as top-pp, min-pp and ε\varepsilon-sampling.

  • •

    Algorithmic benefit: Empirically, we show that higher coverage of the truncated search space is associated with better downstream performance. DLE achieves higher coverage than stochastic self-consistency by systematically exploring previously unvisited high-probability branches, leading to stronger reasoning performance.

  • •

    Systems benefit: We show empirically that DLE is more token-efficient than self-consistency. By avoiding redundant generations, DLE produces more complete sequences under a fixed token budget, which translates into practical latency improvements on modern inference systems, especially in memory-constrained settings.

2 Related Work

Our work targets a specific inefficiency in test-time scaling for constrained reasoning: repeated sampling produces many duplicate prefixes and often re-discovers the same high-probability traces. DLE addresses this by (i) enumerating distinct leaves in a truncated sampling tree and (ii) exploiting prefix reuse across branches.

Test-time ensembling and self-consistency.

Self-consistency aggregates multiple reasoning traces to improve accuracy, typically via majority voting on extracted answers (Wang et al., 2023). Follow-up work extends aggregation beyond simple answer extraction to free-form settings, e.g., by letting an LLM compare, synthesize, or select among sampled traces (Wang et al., 2024a; Chen et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024b). Orthogonally, several methods reweight traces using confidence or selection criteria (e.g., self-certainty, filtering) to improve best-of-NN style inference (Kang et al., 2025; Fu et al., 2025). In contrast, DLE focuses on making the sampling stage itself non-redundant, guaranteeing a set of distinct answer traces.

Reducing redundancy in aggregation by pruning.

Early-stopping self-consistency terminates sampling once answers stabilize (Li et al., 2024), and adaptive-consistency allocates variable budgets across prompts and samples (Aggarwal et al., 2023). Path-based strategy reuses partial computation by expanding from promising prefixes, improving latency while maintaining accuracy (Zhu et al., 2024). DLE is complementary with a different mechanism: rather than adapting the number of i.i.d. samples, it deterministically enumerates previously unexplored branches of the same truncated tree. This also connects to broader work on sampling sequences without replacement that aim to avoid duplicates while preserving distributional guarantees (Kool et al., 2019; Shi et al., 2021).

Search-based decoding.

Beam search (Lowerre, 1976; Sutskever et al., 2014) makes the decoding tree explicit but suffers from degeneration and low diversity; diverse beam search addresses this by adding diversity-promoting terms (Vijayakumar et al., 2016). Other approaches promote beam diversity, e.g., via arithmetic coding style constructions (Vilnis et al., 2023). DLE differs from per-step breadth-first search. It traverses the pruned tree in a depth-first-like manner (greedy completions) and allocates a leaf budget to distinct trajectories, which is particularly well-matched to self-consistency-style voting in constrained domains.

Tree-based structures.

Tree-of-thought style inference explores multiple reasoning paths with self-evaluation (Yao et al., 2023). However, it requires repeated model prompting for each branch. Entroduction uses entropy and its variance to balance computation and exploration in multi-step reasoning (Zhang et al., 2025), and ϕ\phi-decoding uses simulated foresight paths for globally informed step selection but also requires expensive extra computation (Xu et al., 2025). DLE is cheaper by using only next-token probabilities and spends compute primarily on full leaf completions rather than partial rollouts plus re-ranking.

Efficiency via prefix reuse and decoding systems.

Efficient implementations for multi-branch decoding leverage shared prefixes and specialized kernels or KV-cache data structures (Yao et al., 2024; Juravsky et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2024). Trie-based decoding for beam search similarly shares KV cache across beams with common prefixes (Chan et al., 2025). DLE directly relates to these system optimizations because its exploration is explicitly tree-structured, which reuses the longest available prefix.

3 Distinct Leaf Enumeration for Truncated Sampling Distributions

In this section, we first introduce truncated sampling distributions generally, then, we motivate coverage as a metric. Finally, we introduce our distinct leaf enumeration algorithm.

3.1 Truncated Sampling Distributions

Here, we introduce truncated sampling distributions. Let pt(⋅∣𝐱<t)p_{t}(\cdot\mid{\mathbf{x}}_{<t}) denote the next-token distribution of the model at step tt given a prefix 𝐱<t{\mathbf{x}}_{<t} over vocabulary 𝒱\mathcal{V}. A truncation rule defines a so-called active set A(𝐱<t)={v∈𝒱:C(pt(⋅∣𝐱<t),v)}A({\mathbf{x}}_{<t})=\{v\in\mathcal{V}:C(p_{t}(\cdot\mid{\mathbf{x}}_{<t}),v)\} consisting of tokens that fulfill a criterion CC. Then, we can define the resulting truncated distribution qq as follows

q⁡(v∣𝐱<t)={𝟙[v=g(𝐱<t)]if ​|A⁡(𝐱<t)|≤1,pt​(v∣𝐱<t)Z⁡(𝐱<t)𝟙[v∈A(𝐱<t)]if ​|A⁡(𝐱<t)|≥2,\displaystyle q(v\mid{\mathbf{x}}_{<t})=\begin{cases}\mathbb{1}[v=g({\mathbf{x}}_{<t})]&\text{if }|A({\mathbf{x}}_{<t})|\leq 1,\\ \dfrac{p_{t}(v\mid{\mathbf{x}}_{<t})}{Z({\mathbf{x}}_{<t})}\mathbb{1}[v\in A({\mathbf{x}}_{<t})]&\text{if }|A({\mathbf{x}}_{<t})|\geq 2,\end{cases} (1)

where g⁡(𝐱<t)≔arg⁡maxu​pt​(u∣𝐱<t)g({\mathbf{x}}_{<t})\coloneqq\arg\max_{u}p_{t}(u\mid{\mathbf{x}}_{<t}), 𝟙\mathbb{1} is the indicator function, and the normalization constant is given by Z⁡(𝐱<t)=∑v∈A⁡(𝐱<t)pt​(v∣𝐱<t)Z({\mathbf{x}}_{<t})=\sum_{v\in A({\mathbf{x}}_{<t})}p_{t}(v\mid{\mathbf{x}}_{<t}). For a sequence 𝐱1:T∈𝒱T{\mathbf{x}}_{1:T}\in\mathcal{V}^{T}, the probability under the truncated distribution is the product of the conditional probabilities of Equation 1, Q(𝐱1:T)=∏t=1Tq(𝐱t∣𝐱<t).Q({\mathbf{x}}_{1:T})\;=\;\prod_{t=1}^{T}q({\mathbf{x}}_{t}\mid{\mathbf{x}}_{<t}). Typically, CC removes low probability tokens from the sampling distribution which are found to correlate with large epistemic uncertainty Li et al. (2026).

Top-kk sampling (Fan et al., 2018).

Top-kk sampling retains the kk highest-probability tokens under pt(⋅∣x<t)p_{t}(\cdot\mid x_{<t}). Let π𝐱<t\pi_{{\mathbf{x}}_{<t}} be a permutation of the vocabulary such that pt​(π𝐱<t​(1)∣𝐱<t)≥⋯≥pt​(π𝐱<t​(|𝒱|)∣𝐱<t)p_{t}(\pi_{{\mathbf{x}}_{<t}}(1)\mid{\mathbf{x}}_{<t})\geq\cdots\geq p_{t}(\pi_{{\mathbf{x}}_{<t}}(|\mathcal{V}|)\mid{\mathbf{x}}_{<t}). Then, C(pt(⋅∣𝐱<t),v)=𝟙[v∈{πx<t(1),…,πx<t(k)}]C(p_{t}(\cdot\mid{\mathbf{x}}_{<t}),v)=\mathbb{1}[v\in\{\pi_{x_{<t}}(1),\dots,\pi_{x_{<t}}(k)\}].

Top-pp sampling (Holtzman et al., 2020).

top-pp retains the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative mass exceeds a threshold p∈(0,1]p\in(0,1]. C(pt(⋅∣𝐱<t),v)C(p_{t}(\cdot\mid{\mathbf{x}}_{<t}),v) is as for top-kk sampling above, but k=arg​minl∑j=1lpt(π𝐱<t(j)∣𝐱<t)≥pk=\argmin_{l}\sum_{j=1}^{l}p_{t}(\pi_{{\mathbf{x}}_{<t}}(j)\mid{\mathbf{x}}_{<t})\geq p.

min-pp sampling uses a relative threshold which retains all tokens whose probability is at least a fraction pminp_{\min} of the most likely token. C(pt(⋅,𝐱<t),v)=𝟙[pt(v∣𝐱<t)≥pminmaxu∈𝒱pt(u∣𝐱<t)],C(p_{t}(\cdot,{\mathbf{x}}_{<t}),v)=\mathbb{1}\!\left[p_{t}(v\mid{\mathbf{x}}_{<t})\geq p_{\min}\max_{u\in\mathcal{V}}p_{t}(u\mid{\mathbf{x}}_{<t})\right], where pmin∈(0,1]p_{\min}\in(0,1].

At each generation step, ε\varepsilon-sampling only keeps tokens whose probability exceeds a fixed threshold ε\varepsilon. 3.2 Coverage

Here, we define coverage as the probability mass captured by a selected set of sequences under a truncated sequence distribution.

Definition 3.1 (Coverage). Let ℒ′\mathcal{L}^{\prime} be any set of sequences sampled from a distribution QQ (which does not necessarily need to be a truncated distribution). We define the coverage mkm_{k} of a set of sequences ℒ′\mathcal{L}^{\prime} with |ℒ′|=k|\mathcal{L}^{\prime}|=k as its probability mass under the truncated sampling distribution QQ as follows,

mk​(ℒ′)=∑𝐱∈ℒ′Q⁡(𝐱).\displaystyle m_{k}(\mathcal{L}^{\prime})=\sum_{{\mathbf{x}}\in\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}Q({\mathbf{x}}). (2)

Empirically, coverage is indicative of performance. In Figure 3 we find that coverage is positively correlated with performance across ε\varepsilon-sampling, top-pp sampling, and min-pp sampling. We provide more details in Section 4.1. Next, we remark two properties of coverage.

Remark 3.1 (Maximizing coverage over sequences).

Let ℒ\mathcal{L} denote the set of all sequences that have non-zero probability mass. Then, the maximizer of the coverage, i.e., arg​maxℒ′⁡mk​(ℒ′)\argmax_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}m_{k}(\mathcal{L}^{\prime}) is the set of the kk distinct highest-probability sequences out of ℒ\mathcal{L}.

Remark 3.2 (Diminishing returns of expected coverage).

Expected coverage 𝔼​[mk​(ℒ)]\mathbb{E}[m_{k}(\mathcal{L})] (expectation over kk sequences of QQ) leads to diminishing returns with increasing kk due to sampling duplicate sequences. Specifically, the benefit of adding a new sequence k+1k+1 is decreasing. See Section C.1.

3.3 Distinct Leaf Enumeration (DLE)

DLE is our proposed tree-based decoding algorithm that operates on the tree defined by a truncated sampling distribution (see above). Specifically, the nodes in the tree 𝐱<t{\mathbf{x}}_{<t} represent prefixes with active sets |A⁡(𝐱<t)|>1|A({\mathbf{x}}_{<t})|>1 and the edges represent the next-token distribution q(⋅∣𝐱<t)q(\cdot\mid{\mathbf{x}}_{<t}). We will refer to this tree as the pruned tree. DLE replaces sampling from qq by a deterministic expansion scheme at a chosen node. It follows these steps:

  1. 1.

    Given a prompt, DLE produces a greedy generation 𝐱1:T{\mathbf{x}}_{1:T} until an end-of-sequence token (EOS) is reached, while keeping track of active sets along the path.

  2. 2.

    DLE decides on the next branching location ii of the tree and picks an alternative token vv from the active set at that position.

  3. 3.

    The alternative token is appended to the prefix 𝐱1:i−1∘v{\mathbf{x}}_{1:i-1}\circ v. Then, DLE produces a greedy generation from that point until an EOS token is reached.

Step 2 and Step 3 are repeated until there either are no remaining active sets with non-trivial size >1>1 or until a maximum of kk leaf nodes have been created. The output of DLE is a set of distinct leaves ℒ′\mathcal{L}^{\prime} and the corresponding weights Q⁡(𝐱)Q({\mathbf{x}}) for 𝐱∈ℒ′{\mathbf{x}}\in\mathcal{L}^{\prime}.

Expanding a node.

A node 𝐱<t{\mathbf{x}}_{<t} is expanded depending on the size of its active set A⁡(𝐱<t)A({\mathbf{x}}_{<t}).

  • •

    Branching case |A⁡(𝐱<t)|>1|A({\mathbf{x}}_{<t})|>1: One child is created for each token in the active set, which has prefix 𝐱<t∘v{\mathbf{x}}_{<t}\circ v, path probability Q⁡(𝐱<t∘v)Q({\mathbf{x}}_{<t}\circ v), and edge weight q⁡(v∣𝐱<t)q(v\mid{\mathbf{x}}_{<t}).

  • •

    Non-branching case |A⁡(𝐱<t)|≤1|A({\mathbf{x}}_{<t})|\leq 1: DLE creates one child from the largest token v=g⁡(𝐱<t)v=g({\mathbf{x}}_{<t}) with prefix 𝐱<t∘v{\mathbf{x}}_{<t}\circ v, path probability Q⁡(𝐱<t∘v)Q({\mathbf{x}}_{<t}\circ v), and edge weight 1.01.0.

For any prefix 𝐱<t{\mathbf{x}}_{<t} on the ε\varepsilon-pruned tree, its path probability is the product of the edge weights on its unique path from root to leaf.

Remark 3.3 (If the number of leaves, kk, is large, the support of the truncated sampling algorithm and the corresponding DLE is the same).

Note that if we explore all branches of the pruned tree, we enumerate all possible sequences 𝐱{\mathbf{x}} of the corresponding truncated sampling distribution with Q⁡(𝐱)>0Q({\mathbf{x}})>0. Thus, their support is the same.

While Remark 3.3 makes a statement about arbitrary kk, it can be practically infeasible to explore the full pruned tree, depending on its size. Therefore, DLE deterministically expands previously unexplored branches of the same pruned tree to avoid generating duplicate leaves. Using coverage, as defined in Section 3.2, we see that, for the same leaf budget kk, DLE allocates more compute towards uncovering new probability mass. Therefore, we can conceptualize DLE as a compute-budgeted procedure to order the exploration of the tree in a way that maximizes coverage (see Section C.2).

DLE expands the branch that carries the largest probability mass seen so far. Each branch with prefix 𝐱<t∘v{\mathbf{x}}_{<t}\circ v is scored as Q⁡(𝐱<t∘v)Q({\mathbf{x}}_{<t}\circ v) and we choose to expand the branch with the largest score. This rule prioritizes exploring branches which currently seem most likely under QQ and, at the same time, is a greedy heuristic for uncovering new probability mass. We provide an example of this algorithm to help understanding, and ablation study on various other branching rules in Section B.1.

Early stopping.

Branch alternatives can differ at the branching token but still lead to the same greedy suffix later (e.g., semantically similar tokens converging under greedy decoding) (Hong et al., 2025). To avoid repeatedly generating the same continuation, we early-stop after the branch point once such a merge is detected (Figure 4). If a branch matches n=10n=10 consecutive tokens from a previously generated sibling continuation, we stop decoding that branch and reallocate the remaining sequence budget elsewhere. Appendix B shows that this rule helps reduce the frequency of identical final answers since over 85% of pruned branches would have produced the same final answer.

3.4 Implementation

In this section, we discuss leaf aggregation rules and the practical implementation of DLE.

Each generated leaf 𝐱∈ℒ′{\mathbf{x}}\in\mathcal{L}^{\prime} comes with its truncated sampling probability Q⁡(𝐱)Q({\mathbf{x}}), which can be used for weighted aggregation with self-consistency. In contrast to Wang et al. (2024a), we find that uniform weighting is the most robust choice (see ablation in Section B.4)

We highlight that DLE explores new branches from previously generated prefixes, so shared prefixes do not need to be recomputed and their KV caches can be reused. In contrast, standard self-consistency generates each sequence independently, repeatedly recomputing shared prefixes. As a result, DLE can benefit directly from inference engines that support prefix caching. vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023) uses automatic prefix caching (APC), reusing cached KV blocks from prior requests when needed. This lets any new request skip computing shared prefixes if they have been cached before. SGLang (Zheng et al., 2024) is built around KV cache reuse across multiple generation calls that is explicitly optimized for tree-based generations, using RadixAttention, which stores KV caches in a radix tree keyed by token prefixes. We show experiments on the performance of vLLM and SGLang in Section 4.3.

3.5 Evaluation Metrics

In this section, we define the metrics used to evaluate our experimental results in Section 4.

Coverage.

We define coverage m⁡(ℒ^)∈[0,1]m(\widehat{\mathcal{L}})\in[0,1] in Section 3.2 over a set of leaves ℒ′\mathcal{L}^{\prime} quantifying how much of the pruned tree or probability mass DLE has explored.

Cache hit rate.

We measure cache reuse over the flattened tree of the kk enumerated leaves. Each leaf corresponds to one generation stream, and we concatenate all streams to obtain a single measure LflatL_{\mathrm{flat}} that includes all repeated prompt and generated tokens. The actual cache hit rate is the total number of cached tokens reported by SGLang (via cached_tokens) divided by the total flat length: Cact/Lflat{C_{\mathrm{act}}}/{L_{\mathrm{flat}}}. The theoretical cache hit rate is the maximum number of tokens that could be reused given the enumerated tree structure, i.e., the length of the longest prefix of a leaf that matches any previously generated leaf (including the prompt): Cth/Lflat{C_{\mathrm{th}}}/{L_{\mathrm{flat}}}.

4 Experiments

This section evaluates the proposed DLE algorithm on reasoning and coding tasks with various truncated sampling distributions (see Section 3). We choose ε=0.05\varepsilon=0.05, p=0.1p=0.1 for min-pp, for top-kk we use k=10k=10 in combination with top-pp, p=0.95p=0.95 which is commonly used in Qwen models (Qwen et al., 2025). We run experiments with the Qwen (Qwen et al., 2025) and Llama (Grattafiori et al., 2024) model families. We test mathematical reasoning with GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), code generation with HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021), and general reasoning with MMLU-Pro (Wang et al., 2024c). We compare DLE to other state-of-the-art parallel reasoning strategies such as DeepConf (Fu et al., 2025), Self-Certainty (Kang et al., 2025), beam search (Lowerre, 1976; Sutskever et al., 2014), and diverse beam search (Vijayakumar et al., 2016). For additional details, refer to Appendix A and Appendix D.

4.1 Coverage and Sequence Probability

Figure 5 plots coverage against maj@kk across increasing values of kk. For both DLE and the corresponding sampling baseline, accuracy improves as more probability mass is covered, indicating that the two methods follow a similar overall coverage-accuracy relationship. The key difference is that DLE moves further along this curve under the same sequence budget. For a given number of generated sequences, it attains higher coverage, which translates into higher performance as measured by maj@kk.

This interpretation is supported by Figure 6 (left), where the per sequence log\log-probabilities are higher for DLE than for the corresponding ε\varepsilon-sampling baseline. In Figure 6 (right), these higher-probability sequences are also more accurate on average. Together, these results provide evidence that coverage is a meaningful metric for understanding performance.

Figure 7 further shows that DLE increases coverage across sampler hyperparameters. The gain is largest when the per-step active set is larger. For example, in top-pp sampling, a larger pp includes more candidate tokens at each step, so the probability mass is distributed across more options. As a result, stochastic sampling is more likely to spend budget on lower-probability branches. DLE, in contrast, prioritizes branches with high sequence-level probability mass and then completes them greedily, allowing it to cover more of the search space under the same sequence budget.

4.2 Performance Improvements

Table 1 shows various performance metrics for DLE with the three investigated samplers top-pp & top-kk, min-pp, and ε\varepsilon-sampling for Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct. We use the same kk as beam size for the beam search method and also test the other methods with kk completed solutions.

We find that DLE improves upon sampling-based self-consistency with the corresponding truncated sampling baseline. We observe the largest improvements for GSM8K (≈3\approx 3-99%) followed by large improvements for Humaneval (≈4\approx 4-77%). Beam search and diverse beam search do not yield consistent improvements as beam size and compute increase (as compared to the self-consistency baseline). This shows their limited effectiveness as a breadth first, per-step tree search algorithm.

DLE (ε\varepsilon-sampling) needs fewer tokens to reach the same accuracy compared to self-consistency.

Figure 8 (left) shows that DLE (ε\varepsilon-sampling) requires far fewer tokens than ε\varepsilon-sampling to achieve a similar accuracy in both majority voting and pass@kk. To reach a performance of ≈34%\approx 34\%, ε\varepsilon-sampled self-consistency would generate >150>150 tokens with ε=0.45\varepsilon=0.45 while DLE only needs <20<20 new tokens on average per question (for each of the 32 sequences) for similar performance. Larger ε\varepsilon results in more prefix reuse as branching happens later. This is also reflected in a higher theoretical cache reuse rate in Figure 9 (left). For small ε\varepsilon values, the performance plateaus for DLE while it degrades for ε\varepsilon-sampling.

DLE (ε\varepsilon-sampling) achieves higher accuracy than ε\varepsilon-sampling for a fixed token budget.

Fixing the token budget for each question, DLE (ε\varepsilon-sampling) can complete more sequences by reusing prefixes, therefore producing a larger number of final answers for majority voting as shown in Figure 8 (right). At low token budgets, this effect leads to significant gains for DLE.

4.3 Inference Speed

In Section 3.4, we highlighted prefix reuse as a major factor responsible for the efficiency of DLE. Figure 9 (left) details the cache hit rate for DLE (ε\varepsilon-sampling) and self-consistency. We find that DLE shows a higher cache hit rate because answer prefixes can be reused. In contrast, baseline ε\varepsilon-sampling can only reuse k−1k-1 of all kk question prompts. All answer tokens have to be generated. Further, the actual cache hit rate (solid) is very close to the theoretical cache hit rate (dashed) as SGLang effectively retrieves the relevant KV cache from memory. In Section D.3, we compare runtimes for vLLM and provide additional results.

In Figure 9 (right) we find that DLE (ε\varepsilon-sampling) achieves lower runtime on the SGLang inference engine. This improvement is the most significant for small batch sizes of 11 and 22 where speed gains from parallelizing the generation of all traces cannot be effectively exploited by the baseline approach.

Algorithmic versus systems gains.

DLE leads to benefits at two levels. Algorithmically, it avoids duplicate leaf exploration and improves coverage of the truncated search space under a fixed budget. Systemically, its tree-structured exploration exposes shared prefixes that inference engines can exploit with KV-cache reuse. The latter gains depend on the serving stack, cache management, and batching strategy, and may vary across deployment settings. In practice, DLE is most attractive in constrained reasoning settings, smaller-budget regimes, and cache-aware inference engines, where duplicate exploration is common and prefix reuse can be exploited.

5 Future Work and Conclusion

Future work.

One promising direction is to learn better branching policies that combine sequence probability with task-dependent quality signals. Another is to study adaptive hybrids of deterministic and stochastic exploration, for example by using DLE for high-mass regions and sampling for lower-mass tails. More broadly, the tree perspective may provide a useful interface between decoding and training, since branch points expose localized decisions that could support finer-grained credit assignment than sequence-level rewards.

Conclusion.

We introduced Distinct Leaf Enumeration (DLE), a deterministic decoding strategy that explores truncated decoding trees without repeatedly sampling duplicate traces. Across reasoning and coding tasks, DLE improves coverage of the truncated search space and translates this into better performance and practical efficiency gains. More broadly, our results suggest that effective test-time scaling depends not only on generating more samples, but also on allocating computation more efficiently across plausible continuations.

Appendix A Datasets and Parameters

MMLU-Pro (Wang et al., 2024c) metrics are weighted by the number of questions in each category.

All plotted diagrams and tables use Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct unless stated otherwise. All experiments are run on B200 or H100 GPUs using vLLM. The default benchmark for diagrams is GSM8K unless stated otherwise.

Figure 2 measures repetition rate using only generated answer tokens, excluding the prompt. For each question, we compare kk generated answers and count repeated prefix tokens: a token is counted as repeated if it belongs to an initial prefix of length mm that matches the first mm tokens of any earlier generation. Per question repetition rate is averaged across all questions in each dataset. Figure 2 uses ε\varepsilon-sampling with ε=0.05\varepsilon=0.05. Higher ε\varepsilon results in higher repetition rate.

Figure 8 (left) uses k=32k=32 and DLE with ε\varepsilon-sampling. The number of new tokens generated is summed over the full dataset, and averaged per question per kk. Since at high ε\varepsilon, DLE does not need to use the full 32-sequences budget to explore the tree fully, its averaged number of new tokens is low.

Figure 8 (right) uses DLE (ε\varepsilon-sampling, ε=0.3\varepsilon=0.3), and a fixed token budget for each question. For each question, sequences are generated one by one (not in parallel) until all tokens are used up.

Appendix B Ablations of the Proposed Algorithm

B.1 Search Algorithms

Figure 10 shows branching variations ProbFirst (main text) and DivFirst for DLE with ε\varepsilon-sampling truncated distribution.

Branching with ProbFirst.

ProbFirst expands the branch that carries the largest probability mass seen so far. Each branch with prefix 𝐱<t∘v{\mathbf{x}}_{<t}\circ v is scored as Qε​(𝐱<t∘v)Q_{\varepsilon}({\mathbf{x}}_{<t}\circ v) and we choose to expand the branch with the largest score. This rule prioritizes exploring branches which currently seem most likely under QεQ_{\varepsilon}. Figure 10 shows the generation of branches in order. With ε=0.1\varepsilon=0.1, ProbFirst first generates branch L1L_{1} greedily after which 3 branch points will appear with path probabilities 0.10.1, 0.270.27 and 0.1860.186. It explores branch L3L_{3} as it is the largest, then the next largest branch L2L_{2}. Then during the exploration for L4L_{4}, two branches emerge but branch L5L_{5} falls below the threshold so it is pruned. The remaining branch L4L_{4} becomes deterministic under ε\varepsilon-sampling at that node (edge weight 1). We can contrast this approach with a diversity-first strategy:

Branching with DivFirst.

The goal of DivFirst is to encourage diversity early in the generated sequences. The branching point is selected according to the earliest token position. This forces early divergence near the root. In Figure 10, DivFirst creates branch L1L_{1} first greedily. Then chooses the top alternative token at the first branch point that creates L4L_{4} during which L5L_{5} is rejected. The next earliest branch points is at L3L_{3}, and then at L2L_{2}.

The branching algorithm described in the main paper is called ProbFirst. In addition to ProbFirst, we test four additional search algorithms

  • •

    DivFirst selects a branching point according to the earliest available alternative token position. This forces early divergence near the root.

  • •

    RandBranch chooses branching points by sampling from the distribution defined by the ProbFirst weights. We define a categorical distribution proportional to the probability mass under ε\varepsilon-sampling and sample it to get the next branching point. This is no longer deterministic, unlike ProbFirst.

  • •

    GlobalProb chooses branches that have the highest global edge weight. Instead of choosing branches that have the highest global path weight so far (from accumulated edge probabilities), it chooses to explore the alternative token that has the highest probability among all the branches explored so far.

  • •

    DFS is Depth-First-Search that starts with greedy generation, but deepest branches are explored first. This prioritizes late branching.

Table 2 shows that DivFirst performs on par with ProbFirst. Other alternative methods are worse without early-stopping.

B.2 Early Stopping

To avoid repeatedly generating the same continuation, we early-stop. For example, suppose we branch at position ii, producing two candidates 𝐱1:i−1∘v{\mathbf{x}}_{1:i-1}\circ v and 𝐱1:i−1∘v′{\mathbf{x}}_{1:i-1}\circ v^{\prime} with v≠v′v\neq v^{\prime}. We greedily decode forward nn steps from the new branch, obtaining a short suffix s=g1g2⋯gns=g_{1}g_{2}\cdots g_{n} where gjg_{j} is the jj-th greedy token after the branching token. If this suffix ss matches the first nn greedy tokens after position ii of any previously generated leaf that branched from the same prefix 𝐱1:i−1{\mathbf{x}}_{1:i-1} (i.e., an earlier explored sibling branch), then we declare that the two rollouts have merged and terminate the current branch.

We provide an ablation that removes the early stopping condition on DLE with ε\varepsilon-sampling. Table 2 shows that adding early stopping generally results in better performance with low cost of additional tokens.

Figure 11 shows that the fraction of wasted tokens remains small relative to the total number of generated tokens, so the heuristic adds little compute overhead. The best nn is around 10–15 and we use n=10n=10 in the main paper.

To quantify whether early stopping prevents redundant answer exploration, we measure:

  • •

    Trigger rate: how often branch-level n-gram repetition heuristic is triggered. How many branches are early stopped, out of all explored branches.

  • •

    Exact suffix match: how often the early-stopped branches would have continued to produce the exact full continuation, if generation had been allowed to continue with no early-stop rule. In other words, among the pruned branches, what percentage are true duplicate races rather than branches that only matched on the initial n-gram but later diverged.

  • •

    Exact answer match: how often the early-stopped branches would have produced the exact same final answer.

Table 3 shows that early-stopped sequences account for only a small fraction of explored branches, with trigger rates below 10% in both settings. This indicates that the branch-level n-gram heuristic is relatively selective. It does not fire often, but instead targets a narrow subset of branches that are especially likely to revisit an already explored continuation. Among the branches that are pruned, exact suffix match is much lower than exact answer match. This suggests that the heuristic is not primarily removing branches that are token-for-token identical all the way to the end. Many pruned branches still differ at the surface-form level after the branch point. However, despite these suffix-level differences, the vast majority of them still lead to the same final answer, with exact answer match above 85% in both settings. Taken together, these results suggest that the early-stopping rule is effective at avoiding redundant answer exploration rather than only eliminating fully identical traces. Even when two branches diverge in their detailed continuation, the repetition signal is often a strong indicator that they will converge to the same answer. This makes the heuristic attractive in practice. It reduces unnecessary decoding on branches that are unlikely to contribute new answer-level diversity, while consuming little additional compute for abandoned branches (Figure 11).

B.3 Diversity and Coverage

N-gram diversity.

The n-gram diversity of a string 𝐬{\mathbf{s}} is defined as the fraction of unique n​-​gramsn\mathrm{\text{-}grams} among all n​-​gramsn\mathrm{\text{-}grams} in 𝐬{\mathbf{s}} (Li et al., 2016). Specifically, Distinct​-​n​(𝐬)=|unique⁡(n​-​grams​(𝐬))|/|n​-​grams​(𝐬)|.\mathrm{Distinct\text{-}}n({\mathbf{s}})={|\mathrm{unique}(n\mathrm{\text{-}grams}({\mathbf{s}}))|}/{|n\mathrm{\text{-}grams}({\mathbf{s}})|}.

We use n=10n=10 for Distinct​-​n\mathrm{Distinct\text{-}}n and early stopping. Figure 12 (a) shows ε\varepsilon-sampling has much larger 1010-gram diversity for ε<0.3\varepsilon<0.3. But that does not lead to better maj@k performance (Figure 12 (b) and Figure 12 (c)). Generally, DLE outperforms the baseline despite lower diversity. This might be because n-gram diversity is a surface-level proxy for variation and is not directly aligned with correctness, so increasing it can change the form of generations without necessarily increasing the probability mass on correct solutions.

Below in Figure 13, we provide the raw data for Figure 7. We draw the same conclusions as in the main text, see Section 4.1. We emphasize that coverage should be viewed as a useful heuristic rather than a universal proxy for correctness. In constrained domains under truncated decoding, covering more of the retained probability mass is often associated with better performance because correct solutions tend to lie among a relatively small set of plausible continuations. However, this relationship need not hold in all settings, especially when correct answers lie in lower-probability regions or when model probabilities are poorly aligned with correctness.

B.4 Answer Aggregation Methods

Since we can obtain per-sequence probabilities during generation, we can aggregate answers by weighting them according to sequence-wise probabilities. However, we find that this method does not result in systematic improvement in performance, compared to weighting all final answers equally, as seen in Table 4.

Appendix C More Context on Distinct Leaf Enumeration

Section C.1 shows that the expected coverage of DLE leads to diminishing returns when increasing kk, while the motivation of DLE is to explore more new probability mass. Section C.2 shows that our greedy choice is locally optimal and minimizes computational cost. Section D.2 shows an extension to Figure 8 (left).

C.1 Expected Coverage

Let ℒ\mathcal{L} denote the set of all leaves in the pruned tree. Let 𝐱(1),…,𝐱(k)∼Q{\mathbf{x}}^{(1)},\ldots,{\mathbf{x}}^{(k)}\sim Q be the kk leaves produced by the truncated sampling algorithm, and let Sk≔{𝐱(1),…,𝐱(k)}S_{k}\coloneqq\{{\mathbf{x}}^{(1)},\ldots,{\mathbf{x}}^{(k)}\} be the set of unique leaves.

Proposition C.1 (Expected coverage of truncated sampling).

The expected coverage of sampling the truncated distribution after kk samples is

𝔼⁡[m⁡(Sk)]=∑𝐱∈ℒQ⁡(𝐱)​(1−(1−Q⁡(𝐱))k).\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[m(S_{k})\right]=\sum_{{\mathbf{x}}\in\mathcal{L}}Q({\mathbf{x}})\left(1-(1-Q({\mathbf{x}}))^{k}\right). (3)

The expected marginal gain is

𝔼⁡[m⁡(Sk+1)−m⁡(Sk)]=∑𝐱∈ℒQ​(𝐱)2​(1−Q⁡(𝐱))k,\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[m(S_{k+1})-m(S_{k})\right]=\sum_{{\mathbf{x}}\in\mathcal{L}}Q({\mathbf{x}})^{2}(1-Q({\mathbf{x}}))^{k}, (4)

which is non-increasing in kk.

=𝔼[∑𝐲∈ℒQ(𝐲)𝟙{𝐲∈Sk}]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{{\mathbf{y}}\in\mathcal{L}}Q({\mathbf{y}})\mathbb{1}\{{\mathbf{y}}\in S_{k}\}\right] (6)
=∑y∈ℒQ(𝐲)𝔼[𝟙{𝐲∈Sk}]\displaystyle=\sum_{y\in\mathcal{L}}Q({\mathbf{y}})\mathbb{E}\left[\mathbb{1}\{{\mathbf{y}}\in S_{k}\}\right] (7)
=∑y∈ℒQ⁡(𝐲)​ℙ​(𝐲∈Sk)\displaystyle=\sum_{y\in\mathcal{L}}Q({\mathbf{y}})\mathbb{P}({\mathbf{y}}\in S_{k}) (8)
=∑y∈ℒQ⁡(𝐲)​(1−ℙ⁡(𝐲∉Sk))\displaystyle=\sum_{y\in\mathcal{L}}Q({\mathbf{y}})(1-\mathbb{P}({\mathbf{y}}\notin S_{k})) (9)
=∑y∈ℒQ(𝐲)(1−ℙ(∀j∈{1,…,k}:𝐲(j)≠𝐲))\displaystyle=\sum_{y\in\mathcal{L}}Q({\mathbf{y}})\left(1-\mathbb{P}(\forall j\in\{1,\ldots,k\}:{\mathbf{y}}^{(j)}\neq{\mathbf{y}})\right) (10)
=∑y∈ℒQ⁡(𝐲)​(1−∏j=1kℙ⁡(Yj≠y))\displaystyle=\sum_{y\in\mathcal{L}}Q({\mathbf{y}})\left(1-\prod_{j=1}^{k}\mathbb{P}(Y_{j}\neq y)\right) (11)
=∑y∈ℒQ⁡(𝐲)​(1−(1−Q⁡(y))k).\displaystyle=\sum_{y\in\mathcal{L}}Q({\mathbf{y}})\left(1-(1-Q(y))^{k}\right). (12)

The marginal gain follows by the difference of two of the terms. ∎

Therefore, while 𝔼⁡[m⁡(Sk)]\mathbb{E}\left[m(S_{k})\right] is increasing in kk, 𝔼⁡[m⁡(Sk+1)−m⁡(Sk)]\mathbb{E}\left[m(S_{k+1})-m(S_{k})\right] is decreasing. This shows diminishing returns for the expected coverage of sampling from a truncated distribution. Intuitively, this shows that the “waste” of truncated sampling comes from duplicate leaves since truncated sampling samples full leaves i.i.d. with replacement.

Connection to DLE.

In contrast, DLE deterministically expands previously unexplored branches of the same pruned tree which largely avoids generating duplicate leaves. Thus, for the same leaf budget kk, DLE can allocate more compute towards uncovering new probability mass.

C.2 Greedy Sampling is Locally Optimal and Compute Optimal

After picking an alternative token at a branch point, we always complete the sequence greedily. For a prefix 𝐱{\mathbf{x}} and a horizon TT, its best continuation is V∗(𝐱,T)=max𝐱′1:T∈𝒱Tlogp(𝐱1:T′∣𝐱)V^{\ast}({\mathbf{x}},T)=\max_{{\mathbf{x}}^{\prime}_{1:T}\in\mathcal{V}^{T}}\ \log p({\mathbf{x}}^{\prime}_{1:T}\mid{\mathbf{x}}), with Bellman optimality recursion (Bellman, 1966)

V∗​(𝐱,T)=maxv∈Aε​(𝐱)⁡[log⁡p⁡(v∣𝐱)+V∗​(𝐱∘v,T−1)],\displaystyle\!\!\!V^{\ast}({\mathbf{x}},T)=\!\max_{v\in A_{\varepsilon}({\mathbf{x}})}[\log p(v\mid{\mathbf{x}})+V^{\ast}({\mathbf{x}}\circ v,T-1)], (13)

where V∗​(𝐱,0)=0V^{\ast}({\mathbf{x}},0)=0. Greedy sampling replaces the term V∗​(𝐱∘v,T−1)V^{\ast}({\mathbf{x}}\circ v,T-1) by 00.

Remark C.2 (Local and compute optimality of greedy sampling).

Greedy sampling v=g⁡(𝐱<t)v=g({\mathbf{x}}_{<t}) chooses, by definition, the maximum next-token probability p⁡(v∣𝐱<t)≥p⁡(v′∣𝐱<t)​∀v′∈𝒱p(v\mid{\mathbf{x}}_{<t})\geq p(v^{\prime}\mid{\mathbf{x}}_{<t})\forall v^{\prime}\in\mathcal{V}, and it generates a sample in TT forward passes.

As an extension to Figure 8 (left) which only shows DLE with ε\varepsilon-sampling for k=32k=32, we additionally provide results for k=8k=8. We draw the same conclusion that DLE uses fewer tokens for the same accuracy.

D.3 Additional Results on Inference Speed

In the main body, we discussed the inference speed benefit of using SGLang, which can output the cached token count for each generation request. However, vLLM does not output such data, so we cannot directly measure its cache retrieval rate. We can still see that there is some speed benefit from using DLE with ε\varepsilon-sampling at high ε\varepsilon thresholds.

D.4 Deep Think with Confidence (DeepConf) (Fu et al., 2025)

DeepConf (Fu et al., 2025) is a test-time method that filters out reasoning traces of low quality when doing inference or after inference. We only investigate the offline version of DeepConf.

Fu et al. (2025) defines the token confidence as the negative average log\log-probability of the top-nn tokens at a given position ii

Ci=−1n∑j=1nlogPitop(j),\displaystyle C_{i}=-\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\log P^{\mathrm{top}}_{i}(j), (14)

where nn denotes the number of tokens considered and PitopP^{\mathrm{top}}_{i} returns the probabilities of top tokens ordered decreasingly at position ii. The average trace confidence is simply defined as the mean over all token confidences.

Additionally, DeepConf introduces group confidence for groups of tokens, bottom 10%10\% group confidence, lowest group confidence, and tail confidence. For voting, DeepConf introduces confidence-weighted majority voting that weights each answer by its confidence, and confidence filtering that filters the top-p%p\% of traces.

In our experiments, we set the group size to 6464 tokens (as opposed to 20482048 for the original work) as we are working with reasoning problems that require fewer tokens. We experiment with p∈{10,25}%p\in\{10,25\}\%.

Table 9 shows results for all DeepConf experiments (Fu et al., 2025) on GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021) with Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct. Table 10 shows results for all DeepConf experiments (Fu et al., 2025) on MMLU-Pro (Wang et al., 2024c) with Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct. We include the best results achieved in Table 1.

D.5 Self-Certainty (Kang et al., 2025)

Self-certainty (Kang et al., 2025) is a method for response evaluation and selection. More specifically, it is a metric that takes the probability distribution of the LLM into account to estimate response quality without additional compute. The general idea is that a larger self-certainty also corresponds to an improved response accuracy. Self-certainty is defined as the point-wise Kullback-Leibler (Kullback and Leibler, 1951) divergence between a uniform distribution and the next-token distribution, averaged over the sequence length,

Self-Certainty(𝐱1:T)≔−1V​T∑t=1T∑v=1Vlog(V⋅p(v∣𝐱<t)),\displaystyle\mathrm{Self\text{-}Certainty}({\mathbf{x}}_{1:T})\coloneqq-\frac{1}{VT}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{v=1}^{V}\log(V\cdot p(v\mid{\mathbf{x}}_{<t})), (15)

where V=|𝒱|V=|\mathcal{V}| is the size of the vocabulary.

Kang et al. (2025) also identifies that score-based voting methods suffer from sensitivity to score scaling. Therefore, they propose an approach inspired by Borda-counts. First, they rank NN outputs of models by confidence, obtaining a ranking (r1,r2,…,rN)(r_{1},r_{2},\dots,r_{N}). Then, they assign votes to these ranked outputs using the formula

v⁡(r)=(N−r+1)p,\displaystyle v(r)=(N-r+1)^{p}, (16)

where rr is the rank of the output and pp is the voting power.

Table 11 shows results for all self-certainty experiments on GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021) with Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct. Table 12 shows results for all self-certainty experiments on MMLU-Pro (Wang et al., 2024c) with Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct.
